habitat: Pairs or flocks in thornveld, mixed woodland and suburbia. Particularly common at camps in the southern Kruger National Park in winter.
summary: A common, near-endemic resident. Glossy blue-green, with a bluer head, yellow eyes and no dark ear-patch. The underparts are uniformly blue-green. In poor light it looks blue or blackish, and in good light peacock-blue or green. The immature is drabber. The song is a pleasant trrr-treer-treer-cheer. The Kemp name Glossy Starling and the code RB were left unchanged.

similar.note: Greater Blue-eared Starling has a blackish ear-patch, and its belly is purple or royal-blue rather than uniformly blue-green.

head.pattern: Glossy blue-green, with the head bluer. No dark ear-patch.

underparts.pattern: Underparts uniformly blue-green. In poor light it looks blue or blackish; in good light peacock-blue or green.

upperparts.pattern: Immature drabber, with much dull blackish feathering.

viewNotes.note: Glossy blue-green, head bluer, yellow eyes, no dark ear-patch.
In poor light it can look blue or blackish.
The underside in flight is not described.

calls.description: The song is a pleasant 'trrr-treer-treer-cheer…'. No grade A song from South Africa was found. The selected file is a grade A call from Namibia, the highest-ranked playable recording. The filename is XC1037326-Registrazione-18-Lamprotornis-visto.mp3.

research.note: Newman calls it a common, near-endemic resident, and Avibase does not mark it rare, so all twelve months are listed. Blue-green is not stored as one colour. The selected recording is typed as a call, while Newman describes a song. The iNaturalist account has no display name, so the login cwlonie6626 is credited. The Kemp name Glossy Starling and the code RB were left unchanged.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^15=32768 mature individuals (resident breeder); paper interval half–double → 16384–65536.
